newsitem.title: GERMANY: German public banks may face EU probe in June.
newsitem.headline: German public banks may face EU probe in June.

text.p: Germany's private sector bank association said on Tuesday it expected the European Union to start investigating in June a long-running dispute over alleged subsidies to publicly-owned banks.

Wolfgang Arnold, deputy director of the Federal Association of German Banks, which represents the private banks, said his association had last week formally rejected a proposal by the Bonn government to settle the dispute in a German court.
"The association has officially rejected the government's proposal," Arnold told Reuters. "I expect the EU will start an investigation into the public banks in June."

The dispute dates back to a complaint filed by the private banks with the EU Commission in 1994 and could call Germany's giant public sector banking system into question if the EU decides to investigate.
The private banks allege 11 billion marks of state capital transferred to publicly-owned regional banks, or Landesbanken, since 1990 constitute a breach of EU subsidy rules.

The Landesbanken are owned by their respective federal states and savings bank associations. They do not offer retail banking but compete with private banks in corporate finance, securities trading and issuing.
Bonn's proposal, which was aimed at averting an EU probe, had been accepted by the public banks.
The public and private banks have failed in a series of talks to reach agreement and banking sources say the row has become increasingly bitter.

But Friedel Neuber, head of the biggest Landesbank, Westdeutsche Landesbank, and president of the Federal Association of Public Banks, on Tuesday again denied that the public banks were at an advantage.

"On the refinancing side we don't have more favourable terms than our competitors, we refinance ourselves exclusively via the capital market which doesn't give us better terms than anyone else," he told a news conference.

Neuber recently caused a stir by saying the more than 600 savings banks, seen as crucial to persuading a sceptical German public to accept the euro, would be more critical of monetary union if the public banking system were called into question.

The federal states in 1990 started integrating their regional housing development agencies into the regional banks to beef up the banks' weak equity capital before tougher EU rules on capital adequacy came into force in 1993.
WestLB alone received four billion marks in fresh equity capital by integrating North Rhine-Westphalia's housing development agency in 1992.
The private banks see this as distorting competition because it enabled the regional banks to obtain capital at a far lower price than would be charged for funds in the private sector.
But there are conflicting statements on how much interest the public banks pay on that capital.

Neuber said on Tuesday WestLB had in effect paid an interest rate of nine percent on the housing agency's capital in 1996, well above the dividend yield paid by the private sector banks which in the years 1992 through 1995 barely exceeded five percent.
The private banks contend that public banks pay just 0.6 percent when, according to EU calculations, they should pay eight percent, Arnold said.
Other banks accused of benefiting from state capital injections are Bayerische Landesbank, Landesbank Schleswig-Holstein, Landesbank Berlin, and Norddeutsche Landesbank.
